title: The Western Schism (1378–1417)
hookLine: rival popes, divided saints, forty confusing years

cards: The pope is finally back in Rome. Catherine's letters, the long wait, the journey home: it's done.

Then the pope dies, and the cardinals meet to choose the next one, with crowds in the streets outside shouting for a Roman, or at least an Italian. They elect a man who takes the name Urban the Sixth.
Later, some of those same cardinals leave Rome, say the election was forced by the crowd, and choose someone else, who settles in Avignon.
Now there are rival popes, each with his own cardinals, each sure he is the true successor of Peter.

teach.b: First, the split. A schism is a tear in the Church's unity, and this one ran right through the West. Kingdoms took sides.
Some dioceses ended up with rival bishops. Ordinary Catholics, trying to be faithful, couldn't easily tell which pope was the real one, and honest people chose differently. Second, the saints.
Catherine of Siena backed Urban in Rome with all her energy. Vincent Ferrer, a Dominican preacher later honored as a saint too, backed the Avignon line for years.
Holy, prayerful people stood on opposite sides of the question.
The facts were truly tangled, and Catholics today honor saints from both sides.

teach.h: A CURE THAT ADDS A CLAIMANT.
teach.b: Third, the attempted cure. A council met at Pisa to end the split, deposed the rival popes, and elected a new one. But the others refused to step down, and now there was one more claimant than before.

teach.h: A COUNCIL AT CONSTANCE ENDS IT.
teach.b: Another council, at Constance, finally untangled it: one claimant resigned, the others were set aside, and a single pope, Martin the Fifth, was elected and accepted.

teach.h: THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.
teach.b: Through all of it, Christians could pray Jesus's words in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "That they all may be one."
It's a prayer for unity, prayed by him, and it held even when Christians couldn't agree whom to follow.

how: Catholics today recognize the Roman line of popes from the schism years as the legitimate one, while honoring saints from both sides, and they pray for Christian unity, especially in the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity each January.

games.q: you're a faithful Catholic in the schism years. your bishop follows one pope; the next town over follows another. what do you do?
o: leave the Church; nobody knows anything.
keep praying and follow your bishop in good faith.
declare yourself the judge of who's right.
games.why: with the facts so tangled, an ordinary believer could follow in good faith. even saints chose different sides, and the Church honors saints from both.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you honestly can't figure out right now, a decision or a question where good people see it differently, and hold it without forcing an answer.
If you pray, hold Jesus's words, that they all may be one, and ask for light; if not, let the confusion be there without fighting it, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Western Schism. The years when rival popes divided the Western Church and saints stood on both sides, until a council at Constance healed the split. Today's word.
